## Background

Malignant tumors are cancerous, characterized by uncontrolled growth, the ability to invade surrounding tissues, and the capacity to spread to distant parts of the body. In contrast, benign tumors are non-cancerous, typically grow slowly, remain contained within their original location, and do not invade other tissues or spread. Breast tumor biopsies are performed on small tissue samples to determine if a suspicious breast tumor is benign or malignant.

## Aim

The aim of the report is to showcase that there is a difference between the attributes of benign and malignant breast tumors.

## Loading Data and Libraries

```{r}
#| message: false
library("tidyverse")
library("broom")
library("cowplot")

biopsy <- read_csv("https://wilkelab.org/classes/SDS348/data_sets/biopsy.csv")
```

## Data description

The biopsy data set comes originally from the MASS package. It is a breast cancer data set from the University of Wisconsin Hospitals, Madison from Dr. William H. Wolberg. He assessed biopsies of breast tumors for 699 patients; each nine attributes was scored on a scale from 1 to 10. The true outcome (benign/malignant) is also known.

## PCA

Principal Component Analysis is a computational method that aims to project high dimensional data points (multiple variables) into a lower dimensional space explained by the principal components, which usually 2 dimensions for ease of visualization. The principal components are chosen to explain where the highest variance is in the data.

```{r}
pca_fit <- biopsy |>  
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>  # retain only numeric columns
  prcomp(scale = TRUE) # do PCA on scaled data
```

```{r}
pca_fit |> 
  augment(biopsy) |>  # add original dataset back in
  ggplot(aes(.fittedPC1, .fittedPC2, color = outcome)) + 
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(malignant = "tomato", benign = "navy")
  ) +
  theme_cowplot() + background_grid()
```

```{r}
pca_fit %>%
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues") %>%
  ggplot(aes(PC, percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "green", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.01))
  ) +
  theme_minimal_hgrid(12)
```

This plot shows how much each PC explains the data. Here we can see that PC1 explains roughly 65 % of the data while the rest of the PCs all explain less than 10. In the first plot it was clear that PC1 showed a pretty clear difference between malignant and benign.

## Conclusion

As expected, the plots shows a clear difference between malignant and benign given by the first principle component.
